## Proposition 13.10
**Statement:** If an equilateral pentagon be inscribed in a circle, the square on the side of the pentagon is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the same circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABCDE be the given equilateral pentagon, with its vertices in cyclic order. Find the centre O, join the required points, and produce AO through O to meet the circle again at F [3.1, P1, P2]. Thus AF is a diameter [D1.17]. Put AB = p and OA = r. All the radii equal r [D1.15], and r is the side of the inscribed regular hexagon [4.15]. Our route is to determine BF and then apply the theorem on the square of the hypotenuse to triangle ABF.

**Step 2.** The equal sides of the pentagon subtend equal minor arcs [3.28]. The five successive arcs must all be minor: a major one would leave its complementary minor arc containing the other four successive arcs, each at least as large as that complementary arc, which is impossible [CN5]. Consequently the five successive arcs are equal, and ∠AOB = 72° [3.27, 1.13]. Bisect each of these arcs [3.30]. The resulting ten equal arcs determine an equilateral and equiangular inscribed decagon [3.29, 3.27]. Let M be the midpoint of arc AB, and put AM = d. Thus d is the decagon side and ∠AOM = 36° [3.27, 1.13].

**Step 3.** Since OA and OF are opposite rays, ∠BOF = 108° [1.13]. Since OB = OF, the base angles ∠OBF and ∠BFO are equal and therefore each is 36° [D1.15, 1.5, 1.32]. The side BF, opposite the greater angle, is greater than BO [1.19].

**Step 4.** Cut off BT = BO on BF, with T between B and F [1.3]. In the isosceles triangle BOT, the angle at B is 36°, so ∠BOT = ∠OTB = 72° [1.5, 1.32]. Hence ∠TOF = 108° − 72° = 36° [CN3]. Also ∠OFT = ∠OFB = 36°. Therefore TF = OT [1.6].

**Step 5.** In triangles BOT and OAM, BO = OA and BT = OM, while their included angles ∠OBT and ∠AOM both equal 36° [D1.15, CN1]. Side–angle–side therefore gives OT = AM = d [1.4]. Together with Step 4 this gives TF = d, and consequently BF = BT + TF = r + d [CN1, CN2].

**Step 6.** Write x² for the square on x, and xy for the rectangle contained by x and y [D2.1]. By the preceding hexagon–decagon proposition, r + d is cut in extreme and mean ratio with greater segment r; hence (r + d) : r = r : d [13.9, D6.3]. The three-term result applies directly to this continuous proportion, giving r² = (r + d)d [6.17]. Expanding this rectangle gives
r² = rd + d² [2.3].

**Step 7.** Since AF is a diameter, ∠ABF is right [3.31]. Also AF = AO + OF = 2r [D1.15, CN2]. Therefore the theorem on the square of the hypotenuse gives
p² + (r + d)² = (2r)² [1.47].
Expanding the squares, we obtain
p² + r² + 2rd + d² = 4r² [2.4].

**Step 8.** Add d² to both sides of the last equality. Twice the equality in Step 6 gives 2rd + 2d² = 2r²; substituting this yields
p² + 3r² = 4r² + d² [CN1, CN2].
Subtracting 3r² gives
p² = r² + d² [CN3].
Thus the square on the pentagon side equals the squares on the hexagon side and the decagon side inscribed in the same circle, as required.

heath_proof_text: Let ABCDE be a circle, and let the equilateral pentagon ABCDE be inscribed in the circle ABCDE. I say that the square on the side of the pentagon ABCDE is equal to the squares on the side of the hexagon and on that of the decagon inscribed in the circle ABCDE. For let the centre of the circle, the point F, be taken, let AF be joined and carried through to the point G, let FB be joined, let FH be drawn from F perpendicular to AB and be carried through to K, let AK, KB be joined, let FL be again drawn from F perpendicular to AK, and be carried through to M, and let KN be joined. Since the circumference ABCG is equal to the circumference AEDG, and in them ABC is equal to AED, therefore the remainder, the circumference CG, is equal to the remainder GD. But CD belongs to a pentagon; therefore CG belongs to a decagon. And, since FA is equal to FB, and FH is perpendicular, therefore the angle AFK is also equal to the angle KFB. [I. 5, I. 26] Hence the circumference AK is also equal to KB; [III. 26] therefore the circumference AB is double of the circumference BK; therefore the straight line AK is a side of a decagon. For the same reason AK is also double of KM. Now, since the circumference AB is double of the circumference BK, while the circumference CD is equal to the circumference AB, therefore the circumference CD is also double of the circumference BK. But the circumference CD is also double of CG; therefore the circumference CG is equal to the circumference BK. But BK is double of KM, since KA is so also; therefore CG is also double of KM. But, further, the circumference CB is also double of the circumference BK, for the circumference CB is equal to BA. Therefore the whole circumference GB is also double of BM; hence the angle GFB is also double of the angle BFM. [VI. 33] But the angle GFB is also double of the angle FAB, for the angle FAB is equal to the angle ABF. Therefore the angle BFN is also equal to the angle FAB. But the angle ABF is common to the two triangles ABF and BFN; therefore the remaining angle AFB is equal to the remaining angle BNF; [I. 32] therefore the triangle ABF is equiangular with the triangle BFN. Therefore, proportionally, as the straight line AB is to BF, so is FB to BN; [VI. 4] therefore the rectangle AB, BN is equal to the square on BF. [VI. 17] Again, since AL is equal to LK, while LN is common and at right angles, therefore the base KN is equal to the base AN; [I. 4] therefore the angle LKN is also equal to the angle LAN. But the angle LAN is equal to the angle KBN; therefore the angle LKN is also equal to the angle KBN. And the angle at A is common to the two triangles AKB and AKN. Therefore the remaining angle AKB is equal to the remaining angle KNA; [I. 32] therefore the triangle KBA is equiangular with the triangle KNA. Therefore, proportionally, as the straight line BA is to AK, so is KA to AN; [VI. 4] therefore the rectangle BA, AN is equal to the square on AK. [VI. 17] But the rectangle AB, BN was also proved equal to the square on BF; therefore the rectangle AB, BN together with the rectangle BA, AN, that is, the square on BA [II. 2], is equal to the square on BF together with the square on AK. And BA is a side of the pentagon, BF of the hexagon [IV. 15], and AK of the decagon.
